title: Clinical Outcomes and Hospital Resource Utilization Among Hospitalized Patients with Obesity and COVID-19 Infection: Insights from United States National Inpatient Sample, 2020–2022
abstract: Obesity has been associated with worse outcomes in patients with COVID-19 infection, but nationally representative data across multiple pandemic years remain limited. We conducted a retrospective cohort study using the National Inpatient Sample database from 2020 to 2022 to evaluate the association between obesity and in-hospital outcomes among adults hospitalized with COVID-19 in the United States. Adult hospitalizations with COVID-19 infection were identified and stratified according to the presence or absence of obesity. Multivariable regression analyses were performed to assess the association of obesity with in-hospital mortality, respiratory support, renal complications, thromboembolic events, sepsis-related outcomes, cardiovascular complications, hospital length of stay, total hospitalization charges, and discharge disposition. A total of 5,934,565 adult COVID-19 hospitalizations were included, of which 1,450,164 patients had obesity, and 4,484,401 did not. Patients with obesity were younger, more likely to be female, and more commonly African American or Hispanic. After multivariable adjustment, obesity was associated with increased odds of mortality (aOR, 1.27; 95% CI, 1.25–1.29; p < 0.001), respiratory support, vasopressor use, sepsis, septic shock, acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO), acute pulmonary embolism, acute deep venous thrombosis, tracheostomy, acute kidney injury, and renal replacement therapy, along with longer hospital stays and higher total hospitalization charges. Mortality among patients with obesity peaked in 2021 and declined in 2022. Obesity appears to be an independent predictor of adverse in-hospital outcomes in adults hospitalized with COVID-19.

title: A new metaheuristic optimization algorithm based on COVID-19: mathematical model and application to pandemic control
abstract: Abstract This paper introduces the COVID-19 optimization algorithm (COA), a novel metaheuristic inspired by the dynamical processes of the SARS-CoV-2 pandemic, including viral transmission, quarantine measures, recovery, and mutation. COA models the search for optimal solutions through a state-transition framework in which candidate solutions evolve as susceptible, infected, quarantined, or recovered, enabling a unique and adaptive balance between exploration and exploitation. To demonstrate its practical utility, COA is coupled with a Bernoulli operational matrix collocation method to solve a complex optimal control problem (OCP) designed to mitigate the dual burden of COVID-19 and associated heart attack risks. The proposed OCP incorporates a novel compartmental model that tracks susceptible, exposed, infected, vaccinated, recovered, deceased, and a dedicated heart attack patient class while simultaneously optimizing four time-dependent control strategies: vaccination, preventive measures, antiviral treatment, and cardiovascular care. The objective is to minimize the total number of infected individuals, heart attack cases, mortality, and associated intervention costs. Prior to applying control, the uncontrolled model is rigorously analyzed: the existence and uniqueness of non-negative, bounded solutions are proven; the basic reproduction number $$\mathcal {R}_0$$ is derived; and the local and global stability of the equilibria are established. The model parameters are estimated by fitting the system to real epidemiological data from Wuhan, China, ensuring biological credibility. Computational results demonstrate that the proposed COA-based discretization metaheuristic approach effectively identifies optimal control profiles, significantly outperforming baseline scenarios. By integrating a biologically inspired optimization algorithm with a comprehensive epidemiological model and solid mathematical foundation, this work provides a robust, gradient-free framework for public health decision-making, offering actionable insights for managing infectious diseases alongside chronic comorbidities.

title: From Restrictions to Reopening: Changing Epidemiology of Midfacial Fractures After the COVID-19 Pandemic.
abstract: The COVID-19 pandemic profoundly affected trauma epidemiology, but data on post-pandemic maxillofacial trauma remain limited. This study compared midfacial fracture epidemiology between intra-pandemic and post-pandemic periods at a tertiary maxillofacial trauma center. This retrospective cohort study included 156 adults with non-nasal midfacial fractures treated intra-pandemic (February 2020 - January 2021; n = 57) or post-pandemic (February 2023 - January 2024; n = 99). Demographics, trauma etiology and context, fracture patterns, associated injuries, temporal distribution, and treatment parameters were compared. 20.2 %; q < 0.001), accidents at home (56.1 % vs. 15.2 %; q < 0.001), and syncope-related trauma (17.5 % vs. 5.1 %; q = 0.034) decreased post-pandemic, whereas alcohol-associated trauma increased (10.5 % vs. Differences in falls, accidents at home, and alcohol-associated trauma remained significant after adjustment for age and sex. Road-traffic, interpersonal-violence, sports, and e-scooter injuries increased numerically but none of these differences were statistically significant after FDR adjustment. The overall time-of-day distribution differed between cohorts (p < 0.001), with proportionally fewer morning and more evening/night injuries post-pandemic. Time to presentation and surgery decreased post-pandemic (respectively p = 0.008, p = 0.001), while no statistically significant differences were detected in fracture distribution or length of stay. Post-pandemic midfacial trauma was characterized by fewer fall- and home-associated injuries and more alcohol-associated and night-time trauma, whereas no statistically significant differences were detected in fracture distribution or treatment modality. These findings suggest that the principal differences between the study periods concerned exposure circumstances and injury timing rather than anatomical fracture patterns. Given the observational design and absence of a directly analyzed pre-pandemic comparator, these findings describe differences between the two study periods without establishing a causal effect of reopening or a return to pre-pandemic patterns.

title: Immune checkpoint inhibitors versus chemotherapy in COVID-19 among cancer patients.
abstract: Objective The impact of immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) on SARS-CoV-2 infection in cancer patients remains unclear. The aim of the study was to compare the incidence and severity of COVID-19 in patients treated with ICIs versus chemotherapy (CT). Methods Retrospective study in adult patients with solid tumors who received at least one cycle of ICI or CT during the pandemic. Patients with hematologic malignancies, concomitant autoimmune diseases, or receiving combined ICI + CT were excluded. The primary endpoint was COVID-19 infection rate (PCR or antigen test) according to the type of treatment received. Secondary endpoints included infection severity according to SEIMC criteria. Differences between groups were analyzed using the chi-square test or Fisher's test for categorical variables. Associated factors were assessed using logistic regression. Results A total of 235 patients treated with ICI (n = 75) or CT (n = 160) were included. The median age was 64 years and 68.9% were men. Most patients had lung cancer and metastatic disease with good performance status. The overall incidence of COVID-19 was 8.1% (12% ICI vs 6.3% CT, χ 2 test, p = 0.132). No significant differences were found in infection severity (33.3% ICI vs 66.7% CT, Fisher's test p = 0.370) or mortality (0 deaths ICI vs 3 CT, Fisher's test p = 0.211). Vaccination was associated with a lower risk of infection (OR 0.2, p = 0.003). On the contrary, comorbidity acts as a risk factor (OR 1.6, p = 0.016). No association was found between the duration of ICI treatment and COVID-19 incidence ( 9 months [66.7%]; χ 2 test, p = 0.103). Conclusions Immunotherapy was not associated with a higher risk or greater severity of COVID-19 compared to chemotherapy. Vaccination showed a significant protective effect, whereas each additional comorbidity increased the risk of infection by 60%. These findings should be interpreted with caution given the limited number of COVID-19 events.

source_records.title: Immune checkpoint inhibitors versus chemotherapy in COVID-19 among cancer patients.
source_records.abstract: Objective The impact of immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) on SARS-CoV-2 infection in cancer patients remains unclear. The aim of the study was to compare the incidence and severity of COVID-19 in patients treated with ICIs versus chemotherapy (CT). Methods Retrospective study in adult patients with solid tumors who received at least one cycle of ICI or CT during the pandemic. Patients with hematologic malignancies, concomitant autoimmune diseases, or receiving combined ICI + CT were excluded. The primary endpoint was COVID-19 infection rate (PCR or antigen test) according to the type of treatment received. Secondary endpoints included infection severity according to SEIMC criteria. Differences between groups were analyzed using the chi-square test or Fisher's test for categorical variables. Associated factors were assessed using logistic regression. Results A total of 235 patients treated with ICI (n = 75) or CT (n = 160) were included. The median age was 64 years and 68.9% were men. Most patients had lung cancer and metastatic disease with good performance status. The overall incidence of COVID-19 was 8.1% (12% ICI vs 6.3% CT, χ 2 test, p = 0.132). No significant differences were found in infection severity (33.3% ICI vs 66.7% CT, Fisher's test p = 0.370) or mortality (0 deaths ICI vs 3 CT, Fisher's test p = 0.211). Vaccination was associated with a lower risk of infection (OR 0.2, p = 0.003). On the contrary, comorbidity acts as a risk factor (OR 1.6, p = 0.016). No association was found between the duration of ICI treatment and COVID-19 incidence ( 9 months [66.7%]; χ 2 test, p = 0.103). Conclusions Immunotherapy was not associated with a higher risk or greater severity of COVID-19 compared to chemotherapy. Vaccination showed a significant protective effect, whereas each additional comorbidity increased the risk of infection by 60%. These findings should be interpreted with caution given the limited number of COVID-19 events.

title: Disulfide bonds stabilize the SARS-CoV-2 RBD and preserve binding to ACE2 following thermal denaturation
abstract: Abstract The Spike protein of severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) mediates host cell attachment and entry through the binding of its cognate receptor, angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 (ACE2). This interaction occurs within the receptor-binding domain (RBD) of the Spike protein and is critical to the lifecycle and fitness of SARS-CoV-2. A rigorous analysis of this interaction is crucial to understanding this viral entry mechanism. In the present communication, a biophysical examination of the RBD, ACE2, and their interaction is presented. These studies led to the discovery that disulfide bonds stabilize and protect the RBD from thermal and chemical denaturation. It is further hypothesized that disulfide bond stabilization preserves the ability of the RBD to bind ACE2 following its denaturation. The present hypothesis is supported by the finding that the RBD retains ACE2-binding activity after treatment to high temperatures (95°C) under non-reducing, but not reducing, conditions. These results suggest a mechanism by which SARS-CoV-2 overcomes environmental stress to preserve its RBD–ACE2 interaction.

title: Multi-Omics Integration Across Regulatory Layers Reveals Candidate Drivers of Severe COVID-19 Immunopathology
abstract: The clinical heterogeneity of COVID-19 is well known but its determinants are not fully understood, and the regulatory mechanisms connecting host genetic risk to the transcriptional signature of severe disease have seldom been addressed in one framework. Peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) provide a convenient way to measure the systemic immune dysregulation seen in severe SARS-CoV-2 infection, yet most transcriptomic studies of this cell type stop at describing differential expression, rather than asking what drives it. In this study, a focused discovery cohort of 10 PBMC transcriptomes (five healthy controls and five severe COVID-19 patients) from the RNA-sequencing dataset GSE152418 processed through a HISAT2/featureCounts pipeline and differential expression was determined using DESeq2. The gene set was then tested against four largely complementary lines of evidence: Gene Ontology and KEGG pathway enrichment; a miRDB based microRNA target-network analysis; genome-wide ChIP-seq data for CTCF in CD14+ monocytes downloaded from ENCODE; and summary statistics from a published genome-wide association study of severe COVID-19. Thus, genes were prioritized on the basis of convergent support from multiple methods as opposed to any one analytical tool. Significant differential expression (padj < 0.01) was found in 1,459 genes. Pathway enrichment repeatedly highlighted two processes: disruption of the mitotic spindle checkpoint and impairment of mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation. CTCF ChIP-seq identified 42,243 binding sites across the genome with about 40% in gene promoters, including direct occupancy at IL6, CXCL2, ACE2, TMPRSS2 and NFKBIA. A reanalysis of the genome-wide association study (GWAS) confirmed the previously reported risk loci at 3p21.31 and at the ABO locus on 9q34.2. When all four evidence layers were combined, three genes stood out, MMP8 (upregulated), and IL23R and CD209 (both downregulated), each supported by differential expression and CTCF occupancy, with convergent support from the microRNA target network (see Discussion). Altogether, we propose a model of how genetic susceptibility, the activity of transcription factors, and post-transcriptional control regulate the immunopathology of severe COVID-19. MMP8, IL23R and CD209 are candidates for future experimental work.

title: Incidence and Outcomes of Bloodstream Infections in Critically Ill Patients with COVID-19: A Nationwide Multicenter Study in South Korea.
abstract: Purpose Coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) increases the risk of bloodstream infections (BSI), but associated risk factors remain incompletely characterized. We aimed to evaluate BSI risk factors in patients admitted to the intensive care unit for COVID-19. Materials and methods This nationwide multicenter study, conducted across 22 university-affiliated hospitals in South Korea, included COVID-19 patients treated with high-flow nasal cannula (HFNC) therapy or mechanical ventilation. Baseline characteristics were compared between patients who developed BSI within 30 days and those who did not. Pathogens were analyzed, risk factors were evaluated using multivariable logistic regression, and supplementary Cox proportional hazards analyses were performed to address time-dependent outcomes. Results Of 573 included patients, 206 (35.9%) developed at least one BSI episode. Staphylococcus species were the most frequent isolates. Gram-negative bacteria became increasingly prevalent over time, while fungal infections were associated with prolonged hospitalization. Multivariable analysis identified chronic neurological disease, higher baseline Sequential Organ Failure Assessment score, mechanical ventilation, prone positioning, and extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) use prior to infection as independent BSI predictors. Notably, although crude in-hospital mortality was significantly higher in the BSI group (41.5% vs. 31.7%, p =0.012), BSI was not an independent predictor of in-hospital mortality in either logistic regression or Cox analyses. Conclusion In critically ill patients with COVID-19, high baseline severity, chronic neurological disease, and pre-infection advanced life support (mechanical ventilation and ECMO) were independent predictors of BSI. Rather than acting as an independent cause of death, BSI primarily serves as a clinical marker of extreme illness severity and prolonged invasive interventions.

title: Contrasting dynamic and mechanistic signatures of Class 3 and Class 4 neutralizing antibodies targeting SARS-CoV-2 spike protein: dissecting molecular determinants of neutralization mechanisms using a multi-pronged computational approach.
abstract: Neutralizing antibodies targeting the SARS-CoV-2 spike receptor-binding domain (RBD) exhibit distinct patterns of potency, breadth, and resilience, yet the molecular mechanisms underlying these differences remain incompletely understood. Here, we employ an integrated computational framework combining structural analysis, conformational dynamics, mutational scanning, binding energetics, and allosteric network modeling to systematically dissect Class 3 and Class 4 antibodies. Analysis of single-antibody complexes (COV2-3835, COV2-3891, COV2-3906) and synergistic dual-antibody pairs reveals a fundamental mechanistic dichotomy: Class 3 antibodies exert localized mechanical constraint strictly confined to the binding interface, whereas Class 4 antibodies propagate long-range allosteric destabilization from an evolutionarily conserved hydrophobic core through the β-sheet core to the RBM loop. Mutational scanning and energetic analyses demonstrate that Class 4 epitopes are anchored by an immutable hydrophobic core exquisitely sensitive to mutation yet conserved across viruses, conferring ultra-broad binding and limited escape potential, while Class 3 epitopes exhibit a plastic periphery with variable sensitivity that creates multiple escape pathways. Predictions show excellent agreement with deep mutational scanning data, validating our approach. Allosteric network analysis identifies β-sheet core residues as essential communication hubs, where convergence of high centrality and extreme perturbation sensitivity establishes critical hotspots resistant to mutation. This multi-pronged framework provides a generalizable paradigm for understanding antibody neutralization mechanisms, predicting immune escape, and guiding rational design of next-generation therapeutics that balance potency, breadth, and resilience.

title: Binding Free Energy Landscape of Different SARS-CoV-2 Nsp1 Variants Interacting with NXF1-RRM: Insights from Molecular Dynamics Simulations and Markov State Models
abstract: Abstract The interaction of the SARS-CoV-2 Nsp1 protein with the host NXF1-RRM domain plays an important role in host gene expression, which influences virus replication and host immune surveillance. Thus, understanding the key factors that determine their binding affinity, such as mutations, is of great interest. In this work, we investigated the effects of three Nsp1 mutants─D33K/E36K/E37K/E41K, L27D/V28D, and R124E/K125E─on its binding to the NXF1-RRM domain using structural and energetic analysis. To quantify the affinity changes, we developed a computational framework for calculating the free energy landscape of protein–protein binding based on the Markov state model (MSM). Our approach is based on fluctuations of the radius of gyration and the root mean square deviation (RMSD) from a reference state. We found that the D33K/E36K/E37K/E41K mutant exerts the strongest destabilizing effect, resulting in greater structural deviation, reduced compactness, and a significant loss of intermolecular hydrogen bonds. In contrast, the L27D/V28D and R124E/K125E mutants retain structural and dynamical properties closer to those of wild-type Nsp1 (WT), indicating that these mutations have a more limited impact on the stability of the Nsp1–NXF1-RRM complex. These results are in good agreement with the previous experimental work. We also used the molecular mechanics Poisson–Boltzmann surface area (MM-PBSA) method to estimate the binding free energy of these complexes, yielding results consistent with the MSM analysis and experimental data. However, the binding free energy values obtained from the MSM method are more realistic compared to the MM-PBSA method, which tends to overestimate binding free energy values or produce unphysically negative results. Therefore, the MSM approach provides a useful framework for characterizing mutation-induced changes in the structural stability and binding energetics of Nsp1–NXF1-RRM complexes.

title: Stability of the HIV cascade of care throughout the COVID-19 pandemic in Europe: Results from the multinational EuroSIDA cohort study (2016-2022).
abstract: BACKGROUND Prior to the COVID-19 pandemic, antiretroviral therapy (ART) coverage and viral suppression were improving across Europe; however, the impact of the pandemic on HIV care remains uncertain. METHODS In-person visits, ART coverage and viral suppression among those on ART were described in the EuroSIDA cohort for each calendar year from 2016 to 2022 and compared across five European regions. Multivariable logistic regression was used to assess factors associated with having an in-person visit and with viral suppression. RESULTS Among 6740 participants, 71.9% were men, 34.9% were MSM, and the median age was 50 years (IQR: 42-56) at baseline (2016). The proportion of in-person visits dropped from 75.0% in 2019 to 67.8% in 2020, increased to 74.5% in 2021 and was 72.3% in 2022. We observed a consistent increase in ART uptake over the years and a slight increase in missing HIV-RNA data in 2020. The odds of attending clinic in person were lower in 2020 compared with 2016 (aOR: 0.81, 95% CI 0.75-0.87) but not in 2021 or 2022, while viral suppression increased over calendar time (p < 0.0001). Compared to Central-Western Europe, the other regions had lower odds of in-person visits (p < 0.0001, most prominently for Southern Europe, aOR: 0.18) and viral suppression (p < 0.0001, most prominently for Eastern Europe, aOR: 0.07). CONCLUSIONS Our study confirmed the resilience of HIV care across Europe during the COVID-19 pandemic, whereas the regional and country differences in clinic attendance and viral suppression highlighted the need to address persisting gaps in HIV care on a national level.

title: Scientific Evolution of Research Trends on Psychological Distress, Anxiety, and Burnout Among Women Healthcare Workers During the COVID-19 Pandemic
abstract: Abstract This study aimed to examine global research trends, thematic evolution, and collaboration patterns in the literature on psychological distress,anxiety and burn out among women healthcare workers during the COVID-19 pandemic. A bibliometric analysis was conducted on 1,210 publications published between 2020 and 2025, retrieved from Scopus, PubMed, and OpenAlex databases. Biblioshiny was employed to analyze publication trends, influential journals, authors, institutions, country-level collaborations, and thematic structures. A substantial increase in publications was observed between 2021 and 2022, reflecting heightened research attention during the peak of the pandemic. The United States and the United Kingdom emerged as leading contributors and central hubs of international collaboration. The literature primarily focused on workplace challenges and mental health outcomes, particularly anxiety and depression, with specific attention to vulnerable groups such as women and pregnant healthcare workers. Keyword co-occurrence analysis identified three major thematic clusters: pandemic impact, clinical research, and psychological outcomes. Thematic evolution analysis revealed a transition from general COVID-19-related studies to more specialized research emphasizing mental health outcomes, vulnerable population, and methodological advancements. This study provides a comprehensive overview of the evolving research landscape on psychological outcomes among women healthcare workers during the COVID-19 pandemic. It highlights key research trends, collaboration patterns, and thematic shifts, while identifying critical gaps that indicates the need for targeted, gender-sensitive mental health interventions. The findings offer valuable insights for guiding future research, policy formulation, and intervention strategies in occupational mental health.

title: Analysing the healthcare impact of the COVID-19 pandemic in hospitals and care homes using whole genome sequencing
abstract: Coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19), caused by Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome Coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) has been responsible for over 777 million respiratory infections and over 7 million deaths worldwide according to WHO in the six years since it first emerged in Wuhan, China. The spread of SARS-CoV-2 resulted in a pandemic and a huge burden of cases within healthcare and community settings. Over the past few years, countries and communities have continued to live with the virus that has now become endemic in the human population. However, initially when the virus first emerged many public health measures had to be introduced to reduce SARS-CoV-2 transmission. These measures were brought into settings such as care homes and hospitals to reduce the number of cases and protect those most vulnerable to infection. To combat the spread and aid in controlling the virus many scientific tools can be used, one of which is Whole Genome Sequencing (WGS). In Scotland, the first epidemic wave of SARS-CoV-2 led to many care homes reporting an outbreak with high cases and mortality. During this time there was limited testing of hospital patients discharged to care homes as testing capacity was being developed. A key question has remained unanswered about possible introduction of SARS-CoV-2 into care homes from hospital discharge patients. In this thesis, most patients discharged from hospitals were ruled out for introduction of SARS-CoV-2 into care homes, highlighting the importance of screening all new admissions when faced with a novel emerging virus and no available vaccine. Only one discharge episode had a genomic, time and location link to positive cases during hospital admission, leading to 10 positive cases in their care home. These findings contrast with the narrative and assumptions made about first wave care home outbreaks. Results suggest other sources were the main drivers behind first wave outbreaks in care homes and these sources need to be targeted to prevent further outbreaks. The method using WGS and clinical data which has been described shows a successful approach to investigating sources of outbreaks and could be applied to other SARS-CoV-2 outbreak settings such as hospitals or used in future epidemic waves. This thesis investigated hospital-acquired SARS-CoV-2 infections in wards at Royal Infirmary Edinburgh during different variant epidemic waves. The highest proportion of hospital-acquired SARS-CoV-2 cases was during the epidemic waves in the pre-vaccination period. This decreased during the Delta wave in the post vaccination period. The median number of tests per day was the highest during the Delta wave and results suggested a combination effect of high testing and vaccination was important to reducing HAI. This highlights the need for strict testing measures to limit the spread of HAI when faced with the emergence of a novel respiratory virus. Larger wards were identified as those with the highest number of HAI cases and were significantly associated with HAI SARS-CoV-2 cases when considering a Quasi-Poisson model. These findings are supported by sequencing data in minimum spanning trees showing high numbers of linked cases in larger wards compared to low numbers of linked cases in the smaller wards. Therefore, specific wards based on size could be targeted with more measures in future respiratory viral pandemics as HAI may be more likely to occur in these wards. Multiple SARS-CoV-2 variant epidemic waves impacted care homes in Scotland, resulting in many infections particularly in older people’s care homes. This thesis investigated SARS-CoV-2 infections in Lothian older people’s care homes during different variant epidemic waves. Throughout the study period there was a decreasing proportion of resident cases in care homes over the pandemic in each successive variant wave. This shows a changing dynamic in Lothian care homes over time, and the addition of sequencing data showed many staff cases in later waves had no genomic links to other care home cases but were more likely linked to the community. This shows the effectiveness of measures brought in to protect residents and supports the use of these strict measures in future pandemics. Larger care homes had the highest number of SARS-CoV-2 cases, which has been shown by others previously. However, the addition of sequencing data to explore the differences in size of care homes showed more sporadic cases in the smaller care homes and more linked cases in the larger care homes. These are important findings for pandemic planning and targeting care homes by size for future measures.

title: Elevated circulating fibroblast growth factor 23 is associated with acute kidney injury and mortality in coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19).
abstract: Introduction Acute kidney injury (AKI) is a key negative prognostic factor for survival in patients hospitalized with COVID-19, but few reliable biomarkers for AKI and mortality exist. title: Respiratory pathogen spectrum and co-infection patterns in patients with acute respiratory infection during and after the coronavirus COVID-19 pandemic: a five-year retrospective study, 2021–2025
abstract: The coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic, caused by severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2), prompted the widespread implementation of non-pharmaceutical interventions (NPIs) globally. In China, stringent containment measures and mass vaccination were maintained until December 2022. This study aimed to characterize the epidemiological features of respiratory pathogens in patients with acute respiratory infection (ARI) during and after the COVID-19 pandemic, 2021–2025. We retrospectively analyzed 9,674 patients with ARI. All patients were tested using a single multiplex fluorescence polymerase chain reaction (PCR)–capillary electrophoresis panel. The panel detects 13 targets—11 viruses and 2 atypical bacterial pathogens, Mycoplasma pneumoniae and Chlamydia . Of 9,674 patients, 5,289 (54.67%) had lower respiratory tract infection (LRTI) and 4,385 (45.33%) had upper respiratory tract infection (URTI), reflecting the case mix of a hospital-based cohort. The pathogen detection rate was significantly higher in LRTI than in URTI (2,939/5,289 [55.57%] vs. 677/4,385 [15.44%]; difference 40.13% points, 95% CI 38.40–41.80; P < 0.001). Mycoplasma pneumoniae was the leading pathogen in LRTI (954/5,289, 18.04%), followed by rhinovirus (618/5,289, 11.68%) and influenza A virus (456/5,289, 8.62%); rhinovirus predominated in URTI (224/4,385, 5.11%). Temporally, both ARI consultations and positivity were suppressed during 2021–2022 (positives/tested: 326/1,180 [27.63%] and 283/1,161 [24.38%]), rose sharply after NPI relaxation (1,486/4,292 [34.62%] in 2023; 1,046/1,913 [54.68%] in 2024), and remained elevated in 2025 (475/1,128 [42.11%]). After adjustment for age group, the odds of pathogen detection remained significantly higher in 2023 (OR 2.85, 95% CI 2.09–3.88), 2024 (OR 4.19, 95% CI 3.01–5.84), and 2025 (OR 2.19, 95% CI 1.53–3.15) than in 2021. Among 79 patients requiring intensive care for severe LRTI, at least one pathogen was detected in all, and bacterial or fungal co-infection was documented in 72 (91.14%), including multidrug-resistant organisms in 42 (53.16%). During the period of stringent NPIs, respiratory pathogen circulation was suppressed and then resurged after NPI relaxation; this pattern persisted after age adjustment. Mycoplasma pneumoniae and rhinovirus were the leading pathogens in LRTI, in which mixed infections were more frequent than in URTI. Severe LRTI requiring intensive care was characterized by advanced age and a high burden of bacterial and fungal co-infection, including multidrug-resistant organisms, underscoring the need for continued vigilance and optimized management.

title: EVOLVING REGULATORY POLICIES FOR ORPHAN DRUGS POST-COVID-19: UK AND INDIAN PERSPECTIVES
abstract: Background: Globally, rare diseases affect around 300 million people, but most of these disorders lack approved treatments. Orphan drugs - pharmaceuticals for rare diseases - represent a special category of drugs, balancing the profit disincentive with the compelling need. The COVID-19 pandemic (2019-2023) has ushered in an era of "warp-speed" regulatory science, with global adoption of rolling reviews, adaptive licensing, real-world evidence models and emergency use authorisations. This has seen significant regulatory changes in both the United Kingdom (post-Brexit Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency, MHRA) and India (Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation, CDSCO). Aim: This article offers an in-depth comparative assessment of emerging orphan drug regulatory policies in the UK and India in the post-COVID-19 years (2020-24). It reviews specialised pathways, incentives, health technology assessment (HTA) integration, equitable access and institutionalisation of pandemic regulatory innovations to rare diseases. Methods: We undertook a comparative policy analysis by way of a documentary review. It utilised data from MHRA and CDSCO open-access databases (2020-2024), India's National Policy for Rare Diseases 2021, WHO technical reports, UK Rare Diseases Framework action plans (2022-2024) and peer-reviewed publications identified by PubMed and Scopus. Key Findings: Post-Brexit regulatory autonomy in the UK has enabled the development of the Innovative Licensing and Access Pathway (ILAP) and refined Orphan Medicinal Product (OMP) designation process, incorporating genomic medicine in genomics England's 100,000 Genomes Project. India's National Policy for Rare Diseases 2021 is a conceptual leap but lacks implementation with key flaws in funding (₹50 lakh cap), Centre of Excellence (CoE) infrastructure and orphan drug legislation. COVID-19 showed rolling reviews and real-world evidence can shorten development by 30-60%, but these approaches have been irregularly institutionalised for rare diseases in both countries. Conclusion: The regulatory focus is on both countries. India needs a Rare Diseases Act, insurance mandate and CoE investment. The UK needs to resolve late NHS funding of MHRA-approved drugs. Capacity building for regulatory cooperation between the MHRA and CDSCO via a memorandum of understanding (MoU) presents a huge opportunity to minimise waste and benefit rare disease patients in both jurisdictions.

abstract: Purpose: This study aimed to provide a comprehensive understanding of adult perspectives on COVID-19 vaccination by examining the relationship between vaccine literacy and attitudes toward COVID-19 vaccination. title: Impact of Covid-19 Pandemic on Nigerian Capital Market: The Imperative of Testing the Efficacy of Efficient Market Hypothesis
abstract: In this paper we reviewed the efficacy of Efficient Market Hypothesis (EMH) on the outbreak of Covid-19 on Nigerian Capital Market. The EMH is a theory based on informational efficiency by the capital markets owing to their quick and instantaneous incorporation of new information. The study tested the market in two parameters: to confirm the randomness (efficiency of the market) using run-test, and to confirm the effect of Covid-19 protocols on some economic fundamentals using regression analysis. The result of the run-test of the daily Nigerian capital market data (April, 2020 to July 2020) revealed randomness within the period under review. The regression analysis however revealed significant relationship between the markets and some economic fundamental indicators (inflation and international price of crude oil) of the economy. The paper concluded that the Nigerian Capital Markets revealed randomness signifying a weak form of EMH as news about the Corona Virus was incorporated slowly but not instantaneously during the period under review, and hence, the pandemic did affect the market. The study also posited that EMH can be tested and validated not only from economic or finance point of view but also from public health view of the outbreak of Corona Virus. The paper recommended that policy makers in the country should devise a proper hedging mechanism to be put in place to mitigate any unforeseen negative market reactions in future as a result of any health pandemic.

title: Virtual Doula Support After the COVID-19 Public Health Emergency: Strengths, Limitations, and Adaptations.
abstract: During the COVID-19 pandemic, many doulas shifted to a hybrid model, combining virtual and in-person support. Little is known about how doulas have adapted their practices to this new model of support. We conducted semi-structured interviews with 20 certified birth doulas from 11 U.S. Participants provided both in-person and virtual doula support. Interviews incorporated the Framework for Reporting Adaptations and Modifications to Evidence-based Interventions implementation science framework to characterize practice modifications and included critical incident technique questions to elicit comparisons between virtual and in-person care. Interviews occurred from November to December 2025, and transcripts were analyzed using inductive thematic analysis. Participants identified numerous advantages of virtual doula support for doulas and clients, including convenience, scheduling flexibility, reduced travel burden, accommodation of client preferences, and increased participation of geographically distant family members. Key disadvantages included challenges with rapport-building, lack of physical touch, reduced effectiveness during birth, and inability to provide hands-on postpartum assistance. Some doulas described how they modified their approach to deliver virtual support. Views on the comparability of virtual and in-person visits varied widely and appeared related to doulas' conceptualization of their role. Most participants viewed virtual birth support as somewhat inferior to in-person support, although exceptions were noted. Virtual doula support offers meaningful advantages such as improved access and flexibility but presents certain trade-offs. Doulas expressed different opinions regarding equivalence of in-person and virtual support. There is a need for rigorous comparative effectiveness studies to inform policy and coverage decisions as virtual doula support continues to expand.

title: Short-term Cultural Evolution in Response to COVID-19: Integrating Quantitative Analysis with AI-Assisted Thematic Analysis
abstract: Using Greenfield’s Theory of Social Change, Cultural Evolution, and Human Development as a framework, we examine psychological, cultural, and behavioral shifts in China during the first 70 days of COVID-19. We focus on three levels—mortality salience at the psychological level, collectivism at the cultural level, and subsistence activities at behavioral level. Our big-data sample consists of over 200,000 social media posts. Quantitatively, we found a significant increase in mentions of mortality salience, collectivism, and subsistence activities, consistent with prior results established in the U.S., Mexico, Indonesia, and Japan, suggesting a universal response to existential threat. Qualitatively, AI-assisted thematic analysis, an innovation of the present study, identified the most frequent recurring themes across three levels, which complemented the quantitative analysis by providing in-depth insight into the COVID experience. A methodological strength was to compare expert human coder to AI coding, establishing both the reliability and validity of AI coding.

title: Long-Term Trends, Disparities, and Changes in Suicide Mortality During the COVID-19 Pandemic Among US Adolescents: A Population-Based Study.
abstract: Purpose Suicide is a leading cause of adolescent death in the United States, yet its mortality trends and disparities remain incompletely characterized, particularly during the COVID-19 pandemic. Methods This study analyzed mortality data from 1999 to 2023 among individuals aged 10-19 years from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention Wide-ranging Online Data for Epidemiologic Research (CDC WONDER) database. Population characteristics of decedents and trends in crude suicide mortality rates per 100,000 (CSMRs) were examined. Mortality changes were compared across the prepandemic (2018-2019), early pandemic (2020-2021), and later pandemic (2022-2023) periods. Results From 1999-2019, 44,426 adolescents died by suicide, mostly among males (77.6%), older adolescents (84.5%), and White adolescents (82.5%). After an initial decline from 1999-2007, overall CSMRs increased markedly from 2007-2019. CSMRs were highest among males, older adolescents, and White adolescents, whereas the fastest increases occurred among females, younger adolescents, and non-Black/non-White adolescents. Regionally, Midwestern and rural areas showed the highest CSMRs and rates of increase. During the early pandemic period, overall mortality declined slightly (-1.23%) but increased among females (+4.22%), younger adolescents (+2.88%), Black adolescents (+21.88%), the South (+4.58%), noncore rural counties (+1.08%), and large central metropolitan counties (+4.81%). The later pandemic period was marked by an overall decline in CSMRs (-8.53%), with decreases across most subgroups, although rates did not decline among Black adolescents (+0.85%). Discussion Adolescent suicide is an escalating public health crisis with disparities that require equity-focused strategies to reverse trends and reduce gaps.

title: Hyperinflammatory nutritional index as an exploratory combined inflammatory and nutritional marker: associations with cytokines and β2-microglobulin in COVID-19.
abstract: Background COVID-19 is characterized by heterogeneous clinical presentations, ranging from mild disease to severe hyperinflammatory states. While individual inflammatory biomarkers are associated with disease severity, the clinical relevance of combined immunonutritional indices remains unclear. Methods This observational cross-sectional study included 60 COVID-19 patients categorized as ICU, ward, and outpatient groups. The hyperinflammatory nutritional index (HNI), calculated as CRP × ferritin / albumin, was evaluated alongside cytokines and β2-microglobulin. Correlation and ROC analyses were performed. Results ICU patients exhibited significantly higher inflammatory markers, cytokines, β2-microglobulin, and HNI levels. HNI showed a strong correlation with ferritin (r = 0.945) and moderate correlations with cytokines. ROC analysis demonstrated a high AUC (0.953) for HNI; however, this finding should be interpreted cautiously given the small sample size and potential mathematical coupling. Conclusions HNI appears to reflect the combined burden of inflammation and nutritional status rather than an independent biomarker. Its clinical utility beyond individual parameters remains uncertain and requires validation in larger studies.

title: Discovery of D-peptides that allosterically enhance SARS-CoV-2 3CLpro activity by stabilizing its monomeric state.
abstract: The SARS-CoV-2 main protease (3CLpro) is an essential enzyme for viral replication and a major target for antiviral drug development. While its catalytic activity is known to require dimer formation, the mechanism by which it cleaves itself from the monomeric viral polyprotein remains to be further studied. In this study, we engineered several D-peptides based on a de novo designed D-peptide inhibitor. These peptides bind to the 3CLpro monomer and unexpectedly activate its catalytic function. By enhancing the turnover number, the peptides significantly boost the catalytic efficiency of 3CLpro. Among them, LY11 stands out with high binding affinity (K D = 117 nM) and strong potency of enzymatic activation (EC 200 < 1 μM). Through biophysical and computational approaches, we show that LY11 binds in 1:1 stoichiometry, stabilizing the monomeric state while allosterically remodeling the inter-domain linker of 3CLpro to expand the substrate binding pocket and switch on the protease. These findings suggest new insights into the maturation and catalytic mechanism of 3CLpro. The LY11-regulated 3CL protease may serve as a versatile molecular tool for synthetic biology applications.

title: COVID-19 rapid antigen tests as a surveillance tool for population-wide pandemic monitoring
abstract: Abstract Effective mitigation of the COVID-19 pandemic depended on timely and reliable indicators generated by robust surveillance systems. While monitoring of disease burden and transmission relied largely on established surveillance tools, antigen rapid diagnostic tests (Ag-RDTs) were primarily used for individual diagnostics and to supplement molecular testing capacity. Their potential as a population-level surveillance tool, however, has remained insufficiently explored. We performed bivariate and multivariate time series analyses on a previously unanalyzed dataset containing 14 million population-wide Ag-RDT results from Germany spanning December 2021 to January 2023. The ratio of positive Ag-RDTs was compared with the 7-day incidence, 7-day incidence of hospitalizations, and ratio of occupied ICU beds. Results showed strong temporal correlations, with Ag-RDTs preceding pandemic indicators by 1–3 days, demonstrating significant predictive power. Our findings indicate that Ag-RDTs can serve as effective surveillance tools to support mitigation and monitoring of future pandemics, enabling more timely public health responses.

media_mentions.content: Abstract Effective mitigation of the COVID-19 pandemic depended on timely and reliable indicators generated by robust surveillance systems. While monitoring of disease burden and transmission relied largely on established surveillance tools, antigen rapid diagnostic tests (Ag-RDTs) were primarily used for individual diagnostics and to supplement molecular testing capacity. Their potential as a population-level surveillance tool, however, has remained insufficiently explored. Our findings indicate that Ag-RDTs can serve as effective surveillance tools to support mitigation and monitoring of future pandemics, enabling more timely public health responses. Similar content being viewed by others Introduction Effective surveillance is essential for preventing and mitigating the impact of epidemics, pandemics, and other major public health emergencies1. The coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic revealed critical limitations in surveillance systems worldwide, including insufficient diagnostic capacity, lack of preparedness, and inadequate contact tracing2. These gaps led to delayed and suboptimal responses to outbreaks and underscored the need for rapid, reliable data to enable timely public health interventions3. In Germany, the Robert Koch Institute (RKI), Germany’s national public health institute legally mandated to advise the federal government during pandemics, had established pre-pandemic surveillance tools for monitoring transmission, disease severity, and healthcare capacity impacts of respiratory infections4,5. During the pandemic, the RKI used these to monitor several indicators of the pandemic, including the 7-day incidence, the 7-day incidence of hospitalizations, and the ratio of occupied ICU beds4,6. The 7-day incidence, based on the total number of COVID-19 cases reported within the last 7 days, per 100,000 inhabitants7, provides information about the spread of COVID-19 within the population. The 7-day incidence of hospitalizations allows an assessment of the severity of the disease. Apart from the individual burden of disease, it reflects, together with the ratio of occupied ICU beds, the burden of the pandemic on the healthcare system5,8,9. These indicators contributed to how the risk posed by the pandemic was assessed in Germany (see Fig. S1 in the Supplementary Information for the RKI’s risk assessment over time) and how strategic measures and interventions were implemented4. To counteract the spread of infection, the German government and the federal states decided on a range of pharmaceutical and non-pharmaceutical interventions over the course of the pandemic10. Among other interventions, from March 2021, citizens were provided with free antigen rapid diagnostic tests (Ag-RDT) for the detection of COVID-19 as part of the National Testing Strategy to contain the pandemic, conducted at testing centers11. The aim of this intervention was to identify infections at an early stage to interrupt transmission chains12. Additionally, the availability of Ag-RDTs enabled individual self-empowerment, as citizens could independently verify their infection status and act upon the result immediately13. However, the diagnostic accuracy of Ag-RDTs depends on various factors. At the individual test level, average sensitivities are lower for asymptomatic compared to symptomatic individuals14. Furthermore, assays from different manufacturers vary considerably in sensitivity, indicating the need for appropriate clinical validation prior to deployment14. Also, Ag-RDT performance varied across SARS-CoV-2 variants, as sensitivity differed between Omicron and earlier variants15, and not all tests deployed during the pandemic met regulatory certification standards, potentially introducing additional variability into surveillance-based estimates. These limitations in individual test performance have direct implications for the reliability of Ag-RDT-based surveillance strategies, particularly in mass screening settings. The RKI describes Ag-RDTs as part of a multi-layer approach to reduce infection rates, inhibit transmission, and increase the (molecular) testing capacity13. However, despite their widespread use, Ag-RDTs were not included in the RKI’s overview of surveillance systems and studies used for the assessment and risk evaluation of the pandemic6. The large-scale deployment of Ag-RDTs in Germany provides a valuable opportunity to examine whether population-wide Ag-RDT data can be used to evaluate the effectiveness and predictive power of rapid antigen testing as a surveillance tool. These findings could inform future pandemic preparedness strategies beyond the German context. Due to their rapid availability and ease of use, Ag-RDTs could enable the timely collection and transmission of infection data, playing a key role in the early detection of outbreaks worldwide13,16,17,18,19. Previous studies showed the positive effect of Ag-RDTs as a public health measure to mitigate the pandemic and have investigated temporal correlations between Ag-RDT results and other pandemic indicators. For instance, data from Taiwan in 2021 showed that the positive rate of rapid antigen tests preceded reported COVID-19 cases by several days20. Further evidence suggested that hospitalizations followed positive tests or symptom onset with a lag of approximately 4–7 days21,22,23,24, while ICU admissions occurred 6–21 days after symptom onset25,26,27. Additionally, Ag-RDTs have been examined as a surveillance tool for vulnerable populations, such as residents of care facilities in Germany28. However, the existing literature has several limitations. Many studies relied on simulation models of the pandemic that did not necessarily reflect real-world dynamics29,30,31,32. Other studies were based on populations that were not representative of the entire population, such as school children or residents of long-term care facilities28,33, which limited the generalizability of their findings. Furthermore, several studies only covered relatively short time periods, ranging from several days to a few months, or isolated phases of the pandemic34,35,36, which did not allow for assumptions on the long-term and population-wide effects of Ag-RDTs on pandemic dynamics. In addition, various studies contributed important insights into the broader pandemic context but did not directly quantify the effectiveness of rapid antigen tests as a novel surveillance tool37,38,39. In direct comparison to the paper by Niu et al.20, this study distinguishes itself through a significantly larger and more representative dataset and by analyzing the relationship between the ratio of positive rapid antigen tests not only with case numbers but also with additional pandemic-related indicators. The limitations of previous work highlight the need for population-wide, longitudinal studies to fully assess the suitability and real-world effectiveness of Ag-RDTs as a surveillance tool across different pandemic phases. Here, through the analysis of a previously unanalyzed public health dataset containing more than 14 million real-world, population-wide, and longitudinal Ag-RDT results from across Germany, we investigated the suitability of Ag-RDTs as a surveillance tool and addressed several of the limitations outlined above. Our dataset includes both positive and previously inaccessible negative test results. More specifically, we investigated the extent to which the ratio of positive rapid antigen tests reflected the spread of COVID-19, the severity of COVID-19, and the burden on the healthcare system during the pandemic. Our analysis covered the period between December 27, 2021, and January 22, 2023. Results In order to test the suitability of Ag-RDT data to serve as a robust surveillance tool, data derived from phases 7 and 8 of the COVID-19 pandemic in Germany were analyzed40. The full dataset contains 14,817,173 Ag-RDT results collected at testing centers across Germany, with further descriptive statistics provided in Table S1. For the analyses reported in this manuscript, the data were restricted to 9,205,328 tests collected between calendar week (CW) 52/2021 and CW 3/2023, corresponding to phases 7 and 8 of the pandemic as defined by the RKI4. This period was selected as it contained over 96% of all positive test results, ensuring that the analysis captured the most relevant testing activity. Phase 7 (CW 52/2021-CW 21/2022) was dominated by the Omicron sub-variants BA.1/BA.2 and comprised 7,043,003 tests, while phase 8 (CW 22/2022-CW 3/2023) was characterized by BA.5 and comprised 2,162,325 tests. Figure 1 shows the time series of the ratio of positive rapid antigen tests, the 7-day incidence, the 7-day incidence of hospitalizations, and the ratio of occupied ICU beds across both phases. We found that the ratio of positive rapid antigen tests followed a similar trend to the other pandemic indicators in both investigated phases, with the exception of the ratio of occupied ICU beds in phase 7. However, the results between phases 7 and 8 show differences. At the beginning of phase 7, both the 7-day incidence and the 7-day incidence of hospitalizations increased sharply. As a result, non-pharmaceutical interventions (3G regulations) were put into effect in Germany, requiring individuals in public life (including public transport and workplaces) to be either vaccinated, recovered, or tested negative10. Starting from January 7, 2022, additional regulations (2G+) came into effect, mandating that even vaccinated or recovered individuals had to provide a negative test result10. These restrictions were lifted on February 16, 2022, allowing vaccinated and recovered individuals to meet without limitations. Due to declining 7-day incidence and hospitalization rates, most state-mandated measures were withdrawn as of April 3, 202210. In contrast, phase 8 of the pandemic was characterized by the near-complete absence of nationwide measures. As a result, the motivation to undergo testing with Ag-RDTs changed not only within phase 7, but also in direct comparison to phase 837,41. The testing requirements and regulations in phase 7 likely led to testing among a broad spectrum of the population, including symptomatic, asymptomatic, and uninfected individuals. In contrast, in phase 8, when most measures had been lifted, testing was likely carried out more selectively, particularly by individuals showing symptoms of COVID-19. A bivariate time series analysis was used to examine the correlations between the ratio of positive rapid antigen tests and other pandemic indicators, and to assess its predictive power for the other pandemic indicators through Granger-causality testing. A subsequent multivariate time series analysis examined the increase in the predictive value of the ratio of positive rapid antigen tests for the 7-day incidence and 7-day incidence of hospitalizations, as well as the ratio of occupied ICU beds, under consideration of the aforementioned time series. Bivariate analysis reveals predictive power In a first step of the bivariate time series analysis, we calculated the cross-correlation function (CCF) with pre-whitening to investigate the relationships between the time series of the ratio of positive rapid antigen tests and the other time series of the pandemic-related indicators (7-day incidence, 7-day incidence of hospitalizations, and ratio of occupied ICU beds). The significant lags between the time series resulting from the CCF are shown in Table 1. The analysis showed that the time series of the ratio of positive rapid antigen tests was correlated with the 7-day incidence and the 7-day incidence of hospitalizations for phases 7 and 8 of the pandemic. For the ratio of occupied ICU beds, significant results could only be found in phase 8 of the pandemic. To further investigate the predictive relationship suggested by the CCF results, a Granger-causality test was conducted. The results are shown in Table 2. For the 7-day incidence and the 7-day incidence of hospitalizations in phases 7 and 8, the test produced highly significant outcomes, supporting the rejection of the null hypothesis of no Granger-causality. This indicated that the lags of the ratio of positive rapid antigen tests significantly improved the statistical prediction of the 7-day incidence and the 7-day incidence of hospitalizations. No Granger-causality tests were performed for the ratio of occupied ICU beds in phase 7 of the pandemic, as no significant lags could be found using the CCF. In phase 8, Granger-causality was significant between the ratio of positive rapid antigen tests and the ratio of occupied ICU beds at lags of 1–8 days. The results of the Granger-causality test provide statistical evidence that the ratio of positive rapid antigen tests carries predictive information beyond what is captured by the other pandemic indicators alone. An additional figure highlighting the lead times between the ratio of positive rapid antigen tests and the other pandemic indicators can be found in the supplementary material to this manuscript (see Fig. S2). Multivariate analysis confirms Ag-RDTs as independent predictors To implement the multivariate analysis, the relevant model parameters were selected in a first step using lasso regularization (see Table S2 in the Supplementary Information). In a second step, we fitted generalized additive mixed models (GAMMs) based on these parameters. The selection of pandemic-related indicators based on lasso regularization for each GAMM is provided in the Supplementary Information (see Tables S3–S8). The estimated significant parameters of the fitted GAMMs are presented in Table 3. For predicting the 7-day incidence, none of the retained lags of the ratio of positive rapid antigen tests showed statistical significance in phase 7, whereas lags 1, 2, 8, 9, and 15 demonstrated significant effects in phase 8. To predict the 7-day incidence of hospitalizations, lag 6 was significant in phase 7 and lags 1, 8, 9, 11, 15, and 21 were significant in phase 8. Regarding the ratio of occupied ICU beds, significant parameters emerged at lags 4, 10, 14, and 16 in phase 7, and at lags 12, 19, and 20 in phase 8. Furthermore, a comparison of models with different input variables showed that those incorporating the ratio of positive rapid antigen tests best fitted the observed values, compared to other predictor combinations. The results for this comparison are shown in the Supplementary Information. Discussion The aim of this study was to investigate whether rapid antigen tests could be used as a surveillance tool to mitigate and monitor the COVID-19 pandemic. More specifically, we examined how the ratio of positive rapid antigen tests related to other pandemic-relevant indicators for COVID-19 and to what extent this ratio may function as a potential early warning signal. To this end, we conducted both bivariate and multivariate time series analyses. The bivariate analysis identified temporal correlations and potential lead times between the ratio of positive rapid antigen tests and individual pandemic indicators. Additionally, we investigated if the time series of the ratio of positive rapid antigen tests contains information that can be used to predict the other pandemic indicators. The multivariate analysis determined if the predictive power persisted when additional indicators were included in the model simultaneously. The results of the bivariate analysis of the 7-day incidence with the ratio of positive rapid antigen tests showed correlations in phases 7 and 8, which were further confirmed by the Granger-causality test. The observed lags of 1–2 days are consistent with the 3-day lag reported by Niu et al.20, with slight discrepancies attributable to differences in population and prevailing variants. The multivariate analysis showed that lags of the ratio of positive rapid antigen tests were included in the GAMM for phase 7 of the pandemic. This confirmed that the ratio of positive rapid antigen tests had predictive power for modeling the 7-day incidence, even when additional time series were used in the model. This observation was supported by the fact that the model still contained significant lags of the ratio of positive rapid antigen tests when different combinations of predictors were included. The bivariate analysis between the ratio of positive rapid antigen tests and the 7-day incidence of hospitalizations showed significant lags in phases 7 and 8, which the Granger-causality test again confirmed. This aligns with a paper from the US showing hospital admissions lagging case numbers by approximately 1 day21, with minor differences attributable to population and time period. The results of the multivariate analysis also showed that the ratio of positive rapid antigen tests had predictive power, even when other indicators of the pandemic were part of the multivariate model. The results of the bivariate analysis for the relationship between the ratio of occupied ICU beds and the ratio of positive rapid antigen tests showed no temporal correlation in phase 7. In phase 8, however, significant lags could be observed and confirmed by the Granger-causality test. The observed time lag of 8 days in phase 8 is consistent with results from the literature of 6 days from confirmed infection in Berlin25 and 11 days from symptom onset in Sweden26. title: Acute Neurological Manifestations in COVID-19 Are Associated With Complement Activation and Glia-Promoted Neuroinflammation.
abstract: Pathophysiological mechanisms of neurological manifestations in COVID-19 are not fully known yet. In this case-control study, proteomic analysis was used to characterize cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) samples from COVID-19 patients with acute neurological manifestations primarily categorized as: isolated refractory headache (n = 12), encephalopathy (n = 24), and inflammatory neurological diseases (IND) (n = 13). Individuals with non-inflammatory, non-infectious neurological conditions (n = 8) were included as controls. Differentially expressed proteins (DEPs) in neuro-COVID-19 were associated with the complement system, function/activation of microglia/macrophages, inflammatory responses, and neuronal function/homeostasis. Functional enrichment analysis of DEPs and/or proteins specifically detected in neuro-COVID-19 groups indicated activation of complement and coagulation cascades, and synapse pruning in encephalopathy and IND. Upregulated complement activation was confirmed by increased CSF levels of C3a and soluble C5b-9. Biological processes of neuroinflammation, migration of immune cells into the central nervous system, activation of glia cells (microglia and astrocytes), and tissue remodeling were also present in IND. In turn, processes associated with disturbed organization/formation of neuron projections were related to encephalopathy and isolated headache. CSF from patients with isolated refractory headache was enriched for proteins related to neurons and to the cerebral cortex, cerebellum, and basal ganglia. Meanwhile, CSF from encephalopathy and IND patients was mostly enriched for proteins mapped to the cerebral cortex, choroid plexus, and thalamus. Moreover, CSF from IND patients had an increased proportion of microglia-related proteins. These findings support a model in which cases of IND and encephalopathy are associated with blood-brain barrier disruption potentially induced by complement activation and glia-promoted neuroinflammation, resulting in the involvement of distinct brain structures in COVID-19.

title: Genomic monitoring of SARS-CoV-2 uncovers rare in-frame deletion in ORF1a (nsp3) gene: A case report
abstract: Genetic changes in emerging strains of severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) may compromise the effectiveness of laboratory methods used to detect SARS-CoV-2 for the purposes of public health surveillance. We described a case involving a 40-year-old vaccinated male with RT-qPCR-confirmed symptomatic COVID-19 (fever, chills, cough, and headache) whose nasal specimen was collected during routine genomic surveillance; no hospitalization or complications were reported, and therapeutic interventions were not evaluated as part of this surveillance activity. A rare in-frame deletion in the open reading frame 1a (ORF1a) gene was identified using next-generation sequencing on the GridION platform. Sequence data were assembled and analyzed using the Theiagen workflows on the Terra platform. Genome annotation revealed a 69-nucleotide deletion within the non-structural protein 3 (nsp3) of ORF1a. This deletion was identified in only 22 additional SARS-CoV-2 sequences available in GISAID. This newly discovered genetic alteration may have implications for understanding viral biology, including transmission and virulence. These findings highlight the importance of characterizing the functional consequences of rare genomic deletions and evaluating their potential impact on molecular assay performance and genomic surveillance.

title: Antiviral Antibody Fc Dysfunction Is Linked to Increased IgG1 Fucosylation in Long COVID
abstract: BackgroundPersistent SARS-CoV-2 antigen is a leading hypothesis for post-acute sequelae of SARS-CoV-2 infection (PASC), commonly known as Long COVID. Impaired Fc-mediated antiviral antibody function could contribute to inefficient clearance of infected cells and viral antigen despite preserved antibody levels. Therefore, we tested whether PASC is associated with altered Fc{gamma} receptor-mediated antibody function and differences in IgG1 Fc fucosylation, a major regulator of Fc effector function. MethodsSerum samples from RECOVER-Adult participants with prior SARS-CoV-2 infection (99 PASC, 139 non-PASC) were analyzed for anti-SARS-CoV-2 spike receptor-binding domain (RBD) IgG and subclasses, Fc{gamma}RIIIa- and Fc{gamma}RIIa-mediated reporter activity as surrogate measures of antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity (ADCC) and antibody-dependent cellular phagocytosis (ADCP), anti-RBD IgG1 Fc glycosylation, and circulating fucose-modifying enzymes. ResultsDespite higher anti-RBD IgG and IgG1 abundance, PASC sera showed lower ADCC- and ADCP-associated Fc{gamma}R reporter activity, including after normalization for antibody abundance. Anti-RBD IgG1 showed greater fucosylation in PASC samples (30 PASC, 34 non-PASC). Serum FUCA2 was lower in PASC samples (24 PASC, 34 non-PASC), whereas FUCA1 and soluble CD16a levels did not differ between the two groups. ConclusionPASC is associated with impaired antiviral IgG Fc function, increased IgG1 Fc fucosylation, and reduced circulating FUCA2, identifying a glycoimmune axis that may contribute to impaired Fc-dependent antigen clearance and represents a potentially targetable pathway in Long COVID.

title: Association of Race/Ethnicity on Resolving Inactive Kidney Transplant Status Prior to COVID-19.
abstract: Minority waitlisted kidney patients are less likely to resolve an inactive status change. We investigate race/ethnicity-based differences in the reasons for and resolution of waitlist inactivation. The Organ Procurement and Transplantation Network database was queried (December 2014-January 2020). Cause-specific Cox regression and competing risks analysis were conducted to determine the association of inactive status and race/ethnicity, stratified by specific reasons a patient was made inactive. Of the 94,035 patients, 52.5% experienced inactivity. 47.0% were White, 26.2% were Black, and 17.3% were Hispanic. Black and Hispanic patients experiencing an inactive status change were less likely to receive a transplant (White: 43.3%, Black: 27.1%, Hispanic: 30.4%). We analyzed the most common reasons for inactive status: incomplete workup (44.0%), temporarily too sick (25.1%), and insurance issues (11.9%), and analyzed inactive to active transitions. Overall, from the cause-specific Cox regression analysis, we found that there were significant differences in inactive to active transitions: White versus Black (hazard ratio [HR]: 1.19 [1.15, 1.23]), Hispanic versus White (HR: 0.69[0.66, 0.71]), and Hispanic versus Black (HR: 0.82[0.78, 0.85]). For individuals made inactive for incomplete workup, Hispanics had the lowest probability of converting to active status: Hispanic versus White (HR: 0.63[0.60, 0.67]) and Hispanic versus Black (HR: 0.71[0.67, 0.76]). The competing risk analyses yielded conclusions consistent with those of the cause-specific analysis. There are significant racial/ethnic differences in the ability to resolve inactive status. Developing targeted interventions by key stakeholders involved with waitlisted patients may help address this health disparity.

title: Violence, Stigma, and Moral Injury in Nursing During the COVID-19 Pandemic: A Qualitative Analysis From 18 Countries in Latin America and the Caribbean.
abstract: Workplace violence against nurses and midwives intensified during the COVID-19 pandemic, exposing and amplifying longstanding structural marginalization in health systems across Latin America. This study analyzes how different forms of violence were experienced and described by nursing professionals during this period. A secondary qualitative analysis was conducted using text-based responses from an international online survey developed by the Global Consortium, which included 3860 nurses and midwives from 18 Latin American and Caribbean countries. Data were examined through Descending Hierarchical Classification using IRaMuTeQ, followed by reflective thematic analysis for interpretive integration. The analysis identified five lexical classes, reorganized into three interconnected themes: direct violence related to care delivery and system collapse; stigma, fear, and disruption of social belonging; and ethical-political suffering associated with structural blame, moral suffering, and moral injury. Despite contextual differences across countries, narratives revealed recurring patterns of emotional overload, professional delegitimization, and exposure to multiple forms of violence. These findings position violence against nursing professionals during the pandemic as a structural and multifaceted phenomenon rooted in historical inequities and institutional fragility, underscoring the need for sustained policies that strengthen workforce protection, ethical accountability, and institutional support in both routine healthcare settings and future public health emergencies.

title: The Effects of a Digital Exercise Therapy Application for Patients with Shoulder and Knee Pain During the COVID-19 Pandemic
abstract: Objective: To examine changes in function and pain interference among patients utilizing a digital exercise therapy application (DETA) for knee and shoulder pain. Methods: We conducted a retrospective analysis of data from patients utilizing a DETA for non-operative knee and shoulder pain. Primary outcomes for the study were 8-week changes in physical function, measured using the PROMIS-Physical Function (knee pain) and PROMIS-Upper Extremity Function (shoulder pain); and pain interference, measured using the PROMIS-Pain Interference. Data on patient characteristics was used to examine outcomes among specific patient subgroups. Results: We observed a 3.5 point (SD: 7.8) increase in function and a 3.9 point (SD: 7.5) decrease in pain interference overall (p<0.001), with changes in function and pain interference surpassing the minimal clinically important difference for patients with knee and shoulder pain. Patients with knee pain experienced greater improvements in function than those with shoulder pain (p=0.02), as did patients who report moderate-high levels of exertion during exercise compared to those reporting low levels of exertion (p=0.05). We saw greater reductions in pain interference among those with higher education (p=0.03), those with more acute symptoms (p=0.01) and those reporting moderate-high levels of exercise exertion (p=0.02). Conclusion: We observed a clinically meaningful improvement in pain interference and function among patients utilizing a DETA for knee and shoulder pain. Patients with knee pain, higher levels of education, more acute symptoms, and those who reported higher levels of exertion with exercise experienced the greatest changes in function and pain. Impact Statement: This study indicates that self-guided interventions, such as those delivered through a DETA, may be beneficial for patients with knee and shoulder pain. These results may also inform the development of patient profiles that can be used to identify patients most appropriate to receive care through a mobile application.

title: Occupational role, moral obligation and COVID-19 vaccination intent among U.S. law enforcement officers: evidence from a cross-sectional survey
abstract: This study examines how perceived moral/ethical obligation, support for vaccine mandates and primary occupational role predicted COVID-19 vaccination intent among U.S. law enforcement officers during the first week of vaccine availability. A sequential mixed-methods design was employed using survey data collected via Police1.com (December 14–20, 2020; N = 3,124 active sworn officers). Quantitative analyses included multinomial and binary logistic regression with predicted probabilities. Qualitative content and thematic analysis was conducted on 599 open-ended officer comments (645 coded excerpts). Moral/ethical obligation was the near-deterministic predictor of vaccination intent: officers who agreed they had an ethical obligation to vaccinate had 298 times the odds of intending to vaccinate (predicted probability: 96% vs 5%). Mandate support was also strongly predictive. Occupational role effects persisted after attitudinal controls, with patrol officers maintaining 47% lower odds than administrative staff. Qualitative findings revealed that institutional distrust, moralized autonomy and duty-based framing were the primary cultural mechanisms associated with these patterns. The Police1.com convenience sample limits generalizability. Cross-sectional design precludes causal inference. Future research should employ longitudinal designs and collect political ideology and demographic data. Vaccination decisions in law-enforcement appear to be moral and cultural before they are medical. Role-differentiated communication strategies, peer-based messaging and union engagement are more likely to reach hesitant officers than top-down institutional directives. This is among the first studies to examine role-based variation in law enforcement vaccine decision-making using a large-N national sample collected at the precise moment of initial vaccine availability, before any mandate had been implemented. The mixed-methods integration reveals the cultural mechanisms underlying statistical patterns in ways that quantitative analysis alone cannot capture.

title: Family conversations in the context of the COVID-19 pandemic.
abstract: In March of 2020, the lives of billions of people changed. The COVID-19 pandemic was unique as it was an extended event-without a clear end-that involved lockdowns, quarantines, and restrictions, but it was also a time when many parents and children spent large amounts of time together at home sheltering in place. In this special issue, we bring together research from diverse populations across the globe centered on family conversations about the COVID-19 pandemic. The research presented here showcases the breadth of research methods dedicated to family communication, spans developmental periods ranging from early childhood through adolescence, incorporates different constellations of family members, was collected at multiple time points across the pandemic, and examines the mechanistic role that familial conversations may have for child and family well-being. This work has important implications and applications for future widespread societal challenges and, taken together, provides compelling evidence that one way forward may be to focus efforts on resource-efficient and easy-to-implement interventions that target changes in family communication patterns prior to, during, and/or after significant life events. title: Time and Money: Patterns of Nonstandard Work Across the First Year of COVID-19
abstract: The COVID-19 pandemic had a well-documented impact on the formal economy, with the extent of these consequences varying across industries and sociodemographic groups. Less attention has been paid to whether the nonstandard economy, including informal and gig work, mirrored this broader economic fallout. We draw on 2019 and 2020 data from the Survey of Household Economics and Decisionmaking to assess participation in, time spent on, and money earned from nonstandard work across the first year of the pandemic. We find evidence of an overall decline in participation in nonstandard work during this time. However, our results indicate heterogeneous experiences across nonstandard workers: while almost 30 percent reported decreases in time spent on and money earned from nonstandard work activities, roughly a quarter reported increased time and profits. These patterns further diverge across sociodemographic characteristics and types of work activities. Our findings offer insight into the distinctiveness of the nonstandard economy across the first year of the COVID-19 pandemic, with patterns that vary from the formal labor market. These findings further discourage viewing nonstandard work as a substitute for the formal economy during a period of economic crisis, as not all workers may have the monetary or technological capital that facilitates increased profits from nonstandard work activities.
